ABSTRACT Objective This study examined the effect of vitamin D supplementation, sunlight radiationradiation, and home isolation during the COVID-19 pandemic on the seasonal changes in 25(OH)D concentration and selected biomarkers in young soccer players along a one-year training cycle. Method Forty elite young soccer players (age: 17.2 ± 1.16 years, body mass: 70.2 ± 5.84, and body height: 179.1 ± 4.26 cm) participated in the research. Only 24 players completed the measurements during all four time- points (T1-: September 2019, T2-: December 2019, T3-: May 2020, and T4-: August 2020) and were divided into two subgroups: supplemented group (GS) and placebo group (GP). Players from GS received 5,000 IU of vitamin D for 8 weeks (January-MarchJanuary–March 2020). Several biomarkers such as 25(OH)D, white blood cells (WBC), red blood cells (RBC), hemoglobin (HGB), muscle damage markersmarkers, and lipid profile were measured. Results AnalysisThe analysis of the total group demonstrated significant seasonal changes in 25(OH)D, HGB, asparagine aminotransferaseaminotransferase, and creatine kinase along the one1-year training cycle. The level of 25(OH)D concentrationinconcentration in T4 was significantly ( p < 0.001, pη [ = 0.82) higher in both subgroups in comparison to T2 and T3. Moreover, the significant ( p = 0.023) but poor ( r = −0.23) correlation between 25(OH)D and WBC was calculated. Conclusion Current research confirmed the significant seasonal changes in 25(OH)D concentration during four seasons. 8-weekEight-week vitamin D supplementation had no extended effect on the level of 25(OH)D concentration. Introduction The seasonal changes in 25(OH)D (vitamin D) concentration in blood plasma mainly concernsconcern the inhabitants of countries where the sunlight radiation varies according to the season (e.g. Northern Europe, Canada,Canada, and northern states of the USA) [ 2 ]. The largest deficits of 25(OH)D have been observed in people from these areas between October and April when the ultraviolet (UV) index does not exceed 2–3 and the number of sunny days is relatively low. Thus, maintaining the optimal level of this metabolite in blood plasma requires a diet focused on food products rich in vitamin D, appropriate supplementation [ 1 ], and exposure to UV rays [ 3–5 ]. Interestingly, in the countries of North Africa or the Mediterranean basin, a low level of 25(OH)D concentration was also reported. However, these shortages could be explained by the protection against overexposure to sunlight or the use of sunscreen [ 6 , 7 ]. Several authors [ 8–10 ] reported 25(OH) shortages and deficits during autumnduring the autumn and winter in soccer players from southern Poland. Similar seasonal changes were demonstrated in young Russian soccer players [ 11 ], English students [ 12 ], and Swiss athletes from different sports [ 13 ]. In contrast, Brustad et al. [ 14 ] reported that a diet rich in vitamin D might improve its level regardless of the season. The authors stated that high dietary intakes of vitamin D (including fish) mask the effect of seasonal changes in UV exposure during winter. Vitamin D supplementation in young athletes is one of the most important factors protecting against its deficits. Skalska et al. [ 15 ] claimed that a training load analysis during the experiment is an important aspect when investigating the effect of supplementation on the biomarkers. It is essential that both experimental and control groups follow the same training program. Numerous studies have analyzed the correlations between seasonal variations in vitamin D [ 16 , 17 ], the effect of its supplementation on physical performance [ 18–20 ], and bone resorption markers [ 8 , 21 , 22 ]. Nevertheless, the number of researches investigating these topics with reference to blood parameters is still scarce [ 23 , 24 ]. The type of sport is another important factor determining the amplitude of changes in 25(OH)D concentration. The essential issue is whether the training sessions are conducted indoors or outdoors. The meta-analysis by Farrokhyar et al. [ 25 ] showed that the vitamin D deficiency at over 50% of athletes correlated with latitude, winter seasonseason, and indoor training sessions. This observation was confirmed by Maruyama-Nagao et al. [ 26 ], who found that more significant changes in this metabolite were reported in women training inside the sports hall than in women who performed their training in the open air. When the COVID-19 pandemic was announced at the beginning of March, outdoor physical activity was prohibited due to the pandemic restrictions introduced in most European countries. As a result, numerous athletes were forced to perform home-based training [ 27 ]. Grazioli et al. [ 28 ] reported that home isolation significantly and negatively affected soccer players’ physical fitness levels. Furthermore, Hadizadeh et al. [ 29 ] suggested that vitamin D supplementation could decrease the deficiency caused by the lower insolation. According to Jimeno-Almazán et al. [ 30 ], the role of an optimal level of 25(OH)D could be essential to avoid post-COVID dysfunctions. Due to the important role of vitamin D in physiological processes during physical effort in young athletes with deficiency of this biomarker during some seasons, the project considering its changes collectively with chosen blood parameters in young soccer players was introduced. This research aimed to investigate the influence of vitamin D supplementation, sunlight radiationradiation, and home isolation during the COVID-19 pandemic on seasonal changes in 25(OH)D and selected biomarkers in young soccer players along a one1-year training cycle. It was hypothesized that due to the lower sunlight radiation, the highest drop in 25(OH) concentration will occur in the autumn and winter season. Therefore, vitamin D supplementation might effectively prevent its deficiency and negative changes in related blood parameters. However, the home-isolation factor was not part of the design because the COVID-19 pandemic occurred in March 2020 during the project.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of vitamin D supplementation, sunlight exposure, home isolation during the COVID-19 pandemic, and training loads on seasonal changes in 25(OH)D concentration and various blood biomarkers in young elite soccer players over a one-year cycle. It found significant seasonal variations in 25(OH)D, Hemoglobin (HGB), Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST), and Creatine Kinase (CK). While 8-week vitamin D supplementation (5,000 IU/day) showed no sustained effect on 25(OH)D levels, possibly due to home isolation and seasonal factors, it did influence some biomarkers positively. Biomarkers related to morphology, lipid profile, and muscle damage varied more with training loads and seasonal factors than with supplementation alone.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Vitamin D supplementation and Sports Training.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Vitamin D supplementation involved 5,000 IU/day for 8 weeks (mid-January to mid-March 2020) in the supplemented group (n=11), compared to a placebo group (n=13) receiving sunflower oil. This supplementation had no sustained extended effect on 25(OH)D levels beyond the 8-week period, suggesting continuous dosing during deficiency is needed. Training encompassed typical competitive season volumes of 720 minutes/week (mainly aerobic and mixed aerobic-anaerobic drills), increasing to 810 minutes/week in pre-season. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for either the vitamin D or training regimen.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in summer (T4, August), significantly lower in autumn-winter (T2, T3).
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly (p < 0.001, pη[1] = 0.82) higher in T4 (August 2020) for both groups compared to T2 (December 2019) and T3 (May 2020). Largest deficits (October-April) showed 25% deficiency (≤20 ng/dl) in T2. T3 levels were 26.6 ± 6.35 ng/ml (GS) and 26.2 ± 4.52 ng/ml (GP). T4 exhibited highest values, a 34.8% increase from T3, with 22/24 participants at optimal levels. 8-week supplementation had no extended effect; changes were statistically significant and dependent on sunlight radiation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulation of calcium and phosphate homeostasis, bone health, immune function, and overall physiological processes, particularly during physical effort.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: One-year training cycle in young soccer players, seasonal changes in sunlight (UV radiation exposure, highest May-September), home isolation during COVID-19 pandemic, and 8-week vitamin D supplementation (5,000 IU/day).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of vitamin D status and overall health; optimal levels are crucial for immune function, preventing deficits, and avoiding post-COVID dysfunctions. Deficiency (≤20 ng/dl), widespread in autumn-winter, is highly influenced by season and sunlight and can negatively impact health and physiological functions.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Significant seasonal changes; significant increase at the end of autumn (T2) and decrease in the placebo group.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically significant changes observed for the whole group (n=24) over the one-year training cycle (p < 0.001, pη[1] = 0.38 for GS, 0.37 for GP). A significant increase was noted at the end of autumn (T2) when 25(OH)D was low, and a significant decrease was observed in the placebo group (GP). No significant effect of vitamin D supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Oxygen transport in red blood cells, crucial for cellular oxygenation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: One-year training cycle in young soccer players under high training loads (competitive/pre-season), influenced by seasonal changes, 8-week vitamin D supplementation, and home isolation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, relevant for athletic performance and fatigue. Changes primarily reflect training loads, with decreases potentially indicating adaptation or stress, and insufficient training loads during isolation not improving cellular oxygenation.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Significant seasonal changes; changes were similar to CK, showing significant decreases.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically significant changes observed for the whole group (n=24) over the one-year training cycle. Changes were similar to CK, which decreased significantly from T1-T2 (-160.9 U/L) and T3-T4 (-292.7 U/L).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in amino acid metabolism, indicative of liver and muscle health, and associated with muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: One-year training cycle in young soccer players, competitive and pre-season training, and adaptation to applied training loads.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of muscle damage or liver stress; elevated levels suggest tissue injury due to intense physical activity, reflecting adaptations to soccer training.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Significant seasonal changes, characterized by a significant decrease in activity.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically significant changes observed for the whole group (n=24) over the one-year training cycle, with significant decreases in activity from T1-T2 (-160.9 U/L) and T3-T4 (-292.7 U/L). A significant (p < 0.001) time interaction showed a more dynamic drop in the supplemented group (GS, -374.0 U/L) than in the placebo group (GP, -223.9 U/L) between T3 and T4.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme crucial for muscle energy storage and production, released into blood upon muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: One-year training cycle in young soccer players, during competitive and pre-season periods, reflecting muscle adaptation to training loads, influenced by vitamin D supplementation and endogenous synthesis during spring and summer.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A primary and strong indicator of muscle damage and recovery status from physical exertion. Lower concentrations suggest muscle adaptation to training loads, while a more dynamic drop in the supplemented group suggests a positive effect of supplementation in combination with endogenous vitamin D synthesis.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower levels correlated with higher 25(OH)D; dynamic changes observed with lowest levels in T2 (end of autumn) and T4 (end of summer).
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A significant (p = 0.023) but poor (r = -0.23) negative correlation with 25(OH)D concentration was calculated. Changes included a 5.19% increase in T2 compared to T1, and a 4.00% decrease in T4 compared to T3, with a larger drop in the supplemented group (GS, 6.94%) than in the placebo group (GP, 1.14%) in T4.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary components of the immune system, involved in defending the body against infection and inflammatory responses.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: One-year training cycle in young soccer players, competitive and pre-season training, influenced by vitamin D status, seasonal changes in 25(OH)D, and high training loads.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of immune system status and inflammatory response; lower counts in relation to higher 25(OH)D levels suggest a potential immunomodulatory effect of vitamin D, potentially reducing pro-inflammatory effects in intensively training athletes.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Dynamic changes over the one-year cycle, including significant decreases in both groups and a subsequent increase in the placebo group (GP).
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant group or group x time effect from vitamin D supplementation was observed. Dynamic changes included a significant decrease (p < 0.05) in the supplemented group (GS) and the placebo group (GP), with a subsequent significant increase in RBC noted between T3 and T4 in the placebo group (GP).

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates oxygen-carrying capacity and erythropoietic response to training demands. Changes were primarily influenced by training loads, with home-based training during isolation potentially supporting cellular oxygenation.
